Chapter 1: Aroo's Christmas
The story begins at a crossroads, half a mile outside the small West Virginia village of Aroo, where one road leads from New Kensington to Pietown [1], and another leads to Aroo.
Ellery Queen immediately realized that the terrain was important. His first glance revealed many other things, but only found evidence conflicting and confusing. Everything seemed out of place, and it seemed necessary to leave the crossroads and think things over more carefully.
Ellery Queen, the erudite and cosmopolitan man, found himself standing in the cold and gloomy weather of the West Virginia handle region [2] at two o'clock in the afternoon on December 26th, next to an old Duesenberg [3] race car. This unusual phenomenon was caused by a combination of factors, with the most important being his father, Inspector Quin, who advocated working on holidays. The elderly man was deeply engrossed in his daily work, the so-called "police customs," and worked tirelessly. The crime situation in Chicago was always dire, and the police commissioner invited the top police officers from major cities to his jurisdiction to commiserate over the terrible state of affairs.
It was during the trip with his father, the Inspector, from the hotel to the Chicago Police Headquarters that Ellery learned about the perplexing case in Aroo, which was dubbed the "T-shaped murder" by the United Press. There were many elements in the report that piqued Ellery's interest - such as the fact that Andrew Van was decapitated and nailed to a cross on Christmas morning - that prompted him to pull his father out of the smoky Chicago meeting and drive off in a secondhand, fast Duesenberg towards the east.

Saturday morning, there was no sign of activity in Professor Yardley's house, and there was a reason for it. Professor Yardley, like the officials, had received orders; so had his black old maid. It would have been unwise for him to make a public appearance when Inspector Vance and Stephen Magellan were making a fuss and leaving. It was known that Professor Yardley was entertaining a guest - Eliot Quine, a special investigator from New York. If Professor Yardley had appeared alone, it would have aroused suspicion in those who were on guard.
It was a clever plan. Late Friday night, in the darkness that concealed Bradwood, Ellery had quietly driven his Duesenberg car away from Yardley. It was only when he reached the main road that he began to drive like a demon. He then rushed to Minola, where he picked up District Attorney Isam, and they drove to New York.
Saturday morning at 4:00, the old Duesenberg arrived in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. The city had already fallen asleep; both were exhausted and too tired to talk, so they checked into the Sennett Hotel and went to their rooms. Ellery instructed the front desk to call them at 9:00 a.m., and then they collapsed on the bed like corpses.
Saturday morning at 9:30, they were already several miles outside Harrisburg, heading towards Pittsburgh. They didn't stop for lunch. The car was covered in dust, and Ellery and Isam were both exhausted from this tedious journey... The Duesenberg had been performing excellently for years. On two occasions, when Ellery drove the old car at 70 miles per hour, he was pulled over by motorcycle police for questioning. After Isam showed his credentials, they were allowed to continue... At 3:00 p.m., they were crossing Pittsburgh.
Isam complained, "Let all this go to hell. Can't we stop for a moment? I don't know about you, but I'm hungry. Let's eat something."

"I thought you weren't interested," Ellery said, jumping off the sidewalk. "Hey, come here!" he called to a country bumpkin wrapped in a blue work suit, sweeping the sidewalk with a worn-out broom. "Is the sheriff of Arroyo here?" The man stared at him in disbelief. "Of course, it's written on the sign… come on, you crook."
It was a dreary residential area with few buildings. The Duesenberg stopped in front of a building whose skeletal structure was made of shoddy wood, like a box for growing mushrooms in the past. Next to it was a general store with an old gas pump in front, and then a car repair shop. A handwritten sign hung proudly in front of the mushroom box-shaped building: Arroyo Village Hall. They found the gentleman they were looking for sitting at a desk at the back of the building, asleep. The sign on the door read "Town Marshal."
Quinlan snorted, and the town marshal lifted his heavy eyelids, scratched his head, and said in a hoarse whisper, "If you're looking for Matt Hollis, he's out."
Ellery smiled. "We're looking for Arroyo's Sheriff Redden."
"Oh, I am," he said. "What do you want?"
"Sheriff," Ellery said menacingly, "allow me to introduce Richard Quin, the head of the New York Police Department's Homicide Division—he's here in person."
"Who?" The sheriff stared blankly, "New York?"
"Absolutely," Ellery said, stepping on his father's toes, "Now, Sheriff, we want—"
"Sit," said Sheriff Luddon, kicking a chair over to Quin. Quin grunted and sat down elegantly. "This Mr. Van's business, huh? I don't see how the New Yorkers would be interested. What's going on?"
Ellery took out a cigarette case and offered it to the sheriff, who grumbled and stuffed a large wad of chewing tobacco into his mouth.
"Tell me everything, Sheriff."

A panoramic vision unfolded before Ellery's eyes. Due to a terrible oversight, the wheel of fate had turned, and his telegram to Redden was as good as unsent. The man in the checkered shirt patiently explained that the sheriff and the town's mayor, Matt Hollis, had left two days ago for their annual fishing trip; they would be gone for a week, camping out in the wilderness, fishing in the Ohio River and its tributaries. They wouldn't be back until Sunday. The telegram had arrived the day before, a few minutes past three; the man in the checkered shirt—who claimed to be the caretaker, housekeeper, and handyman—had received the telegram, signed it, and placed it on the sheriff's desk, where it might have sat for a week had Ellery not arrived. The caretaker seemed to have something on his mind, launching into a rambling discourse, but Ellery pushed him aside, his eyes filled with a vague fear, and returned to Aroon Street, jumping into his Duesenberg car.
He revved the engine, turned the corner, and drove along the route he remembered from his previous adventure with Esam and Sheriff Redden. There was no time to contact the county prosecutor, Krutem, or the state police's Captain Pike. If the thing he feared hadn't happened yet, he was sure he could handle any situation that might arise; he had a loaded semi-automatic pistol in the pocket of his Duesenberg. If it had already happened…

"Is the sheriff of Arroyo here?" The man stared at him in disbelief. "Of course, it's written on the sign… come on, you crook."
It was a dreary residential area with few buildings. The Duesenberg stopped in front of a building whose skeletal structure was made of shoddy wood, like a box for growing mushrooms in the past. Next to it was a general store with an old gas pump in front, and then a car repair shop. A handwritten sign hung proudly in front of the mushroom box-shaped building: Arroyo Village Hall. They found the gentleman they were looking for sitting at a desk at the back of the building, asleep. The sign on the door read "Town Marshal."
Quinlan snorted, and the town marshal lifted his heavy eyelids, scratched his head, and said in a hoarse whisper, "If you're looking for Matt Hollis, he's out."
Ellery smiled. "We're looking for Arroyo's Sheriff Redden."
"Oh, I am," he said. "What do you want?"
"Sheriff," Ellery said menacingly, "allow me to introduce Richard Quin, the head of the New York Police Department's Homicide Division—he's here in person."
"Who?" The sheriff stared blankly, "New York?"
"Absolutely," Ellery said, stepping on his father's toes, "Now, Sheriff, we want—"
"Sit," said Sheriff Luddon, kicking a chair over to Quin. Quin grunted and sat down elegantly. "This Mr. Van's business, huh? I don't see how the New Yorkers would be interested. What's going on?"
Ellery took out a cigarette case and offered it to the sheriff, who grumbled and stuffed a large wad of chewing tobacco into his mouth.
"Tell me everything, Sheriff."

"Yes. Matt – he's our mayor, you know – Matt and I, we took four boys with us in a car. A mess, he – I mean, Van. I've never seen anything like it, and it's still Christmas. I call it blasphemy. As for Van, he's an atheist."
"Huh?" the officer asked quickly, his red nose poking out from the folds of the scarf, "Atheist? What does that mean?"
"Oh, maybe not an atheist," Sheriff Redden mumbled uneasily, "I'm not a regular churchgoer myself, but Van never goes. The parish priest – well, I'd better not talk about that."
"Quite extraordinary," Ellery turned to his father and said. "Indeed, it's quite extraordinary. Dad, it's like something a religious fanatic would do."
"Yes, they all say so," Judge Redden said. "I—I don't know. I'm just a country judge, you know? This jail hasn't held a vagrant in three years. But I dare say, gentlemen, it's not just about religion."
"I don't think anyone in town would be a suspect," Ellery frowned and asserted.
"Nobody would be so crazy, I tell you, it must be someone connected to Range's past."
"Has there been any strangers in town lately?"
"None... So Matt and I, and the boys, checked the height, build, clothing, and credentials of the body, and then identified him, and put the body down. On the way back to the village, we stopped at Van's house -"
"Well," Ellery said eagerly, "What did you find?"
"It was like hell," Sheriff Redden said, chewing on his tobacco, "There were signs of a violent struggle, chairs were overturned, almost everything had blood on it. The door had a big T painted in blood, as the newspaper said, and poor old Clark disappeared without a trace."
"Ah," said the officer, "Is that the servant who just walked away, huh? Did he take his clothes?"

Sheriff Redden led them up a winding path that seemed to lead into the nearby mountains. "Different road," he said. "You park the car here, and we'll walk up the mountain."
"Walk?" Isam asked skeptically, eyeing the steep slope.
"Well," Redden said cheerfully, stretching out the syllables. "I could carry you, Mr. Isam."
They parked the car in a thicket. The district attorney looked around, then bent over the side of the Duesenberg and pulled out a large bundle from the undercarriage. Redden watched curiously, but neither man said anything.
The sheriff lowered his big head and laboriously pushed through the underbrush, searching for the target with an indifferent air. Finally, he pointed out a hidden path. Ellery and Isam followed silently, struggling to keep up. It was a real climb, requiring them to traverse a wilderness of dense jungle; the trees were so thick that they blocked out the sun. The air was hot, and the three men were soaked with sweat after only fifty feet.
Fifteen minutes of painful uphill climbing, the forest became denser, and the path narrower; the sheriff suddenly stopped.
"Matt Hollis once told me," he grumbled, pointing, "that there's a roof. That's it."
They approached closer, with Rueden leading the way. As the sheriff had said, it was there...in a small clearing in the woods, under a huge outcropping of rock on the hillside, squatting a crude shack. The trees on either side and in front of the shack had been cut back thirty feet, and its rear was protected by an outcropping of granite. Erlie stared, seeing a high protective fence of thirty feet on either side and in front, made of tangled barbed wire that looked dangerous. "Look at that!" Escham whispered. "Not even a door!"

A man in a blue gingham shirt was sweeping the sidewalk in front of the town hall, and Ellery dimly remembered him.
"Hey, buddy," the man dropped his broom and tried to grab Ellery's arm as he ran past, "where are you going? Who are you going to see?"
Ellery didn't answer. He rushed through the dim hall to the rear office of Judge Lutten. The door to the judge's office was closed; as he saw, the fortress of Aroon residents was devoid of life. He tried the door, and it was unlocked.
The man in the blue gingham shirt, with a rough face and a stubborn look, slowly followed him.
The office of Judge Lutten was empty.
"Where is the judge?" Ellery asks.
"I was just about to tell you," the man says stubbornly, "he's not here."
"Ah!" Ellery says, nodding sharply. So, Ludden went into the mountains. "When did the judge leave?"
"What!?" Ellery's voice is filled with surprise, sadness, and despair. "Oh, no, he didn't get my -" He rushes to Judge Ludden's desk. There is a pile of messy papers on the desk. Ellery begins to toss through the judge's official letters – if they are official letters, the man in blue tries to stop him, but it's to no avail. So, as he feared, it lies there, a yellow envelope of a telegram.
He tears it open and reads:
West Virginia, Aroon, Sheriff Redden
Assemble the police force and guard Old Pete's shack until I arrive. Report Crosetto's return to Krutem. If the situation has already occurred when you arrive at the shack, find Crosetto's tracks but do not disturb the scene.
Ellery Queen

Mr. Crocker left the witness stand, grateful, and hurried down the aisle towards the door.
"Hey," the coroner, Mr. Stapleton, suddenly spoke, startling the small man with the brown beard who was cowering in a chair with wary eyes, "you, over there, come up to the witness stand."
The constable stood up, pulling the man with the brown beard to his feet and pushing him forward. The little man walked docilely, but his wild eyes were filled with fear, and he kept trying to shrink back. The constable roughly sat him down in the witness chair and returned to his seat.

The man sat in the witness chair, suddenly the focus of attention, and the audience erupted in laughter again at his strange attire and appearance. It took a long time for the court to regain order. Ellery firmly put his glasses back on. "So we abandon the Egyptian theory altogether! At least that's what I'm doing. The most recent worrying sign is that I keep abandoning my original ideas; my brain must be rusting."

"And," Ellery countered, "faciunt nae intelligendo, ut nihil intelligant...[21] Knowledge is too much that brings about complete ignorance. Of course, not intentionally to anyone—"
"Of course not," Adler said seriously, "Terence[22] didn't mean that, did he?... Anyway, I think you're trying to explain these crimes using Egyptology. chunk_context.text:
"Was Ito killed by the real killer?"
"Yes. The horse was also killed by the same killer."
"This explanation, although cheap, seems well-organized to me."
I observed Mukimizu's reaction, but he seemed to be drinking his coffee in a melancholy manner and said, "So, it's like the plot of 'The Dog Park Murder Case', isn't it? In other words, the horse finally became a victim and was killed accidentally?"
"It seems so." I nodded.
"The horse, who was assumed to be the killer, was not the killer after all. How ridiculous. Well, let's put that aside. Your meaning is that the locked room and the decapitation were also the work of this true culprit, right?"
"It's likely that 'Hell's Gate' was originally intended for Ito. After all, the initial target was Ito. The murderer just gave Hayama's body and Ito's head the 'Hell's Gate' - out of the curiosity you mentioned."
"The overall plot fits well. However…" Wakisugi's words always bring a sense of foreboding, "Why did the murderer cut off Ito's foot? And what does the blood of Hayama found in Ito's room mean?"
"Well…"
Wakisugi quickly posed another question, "Why did the murderer create the locked room? What method did he use? And why did Hayama have the original key to 'Hell's Gate' in his hand?"
Is this his counterattack for my earlier questioning? Perhaps he wasn't asking me, but rather questioning himself.
"You're not making it easy for me! But I can answer the second question."
"How so?" Mochizuki pretended to listen intently.
"Before the decapitation, Uchida was knocked unconscious by a blow to the back of his head. He bled from his nose at the time."
"So that's how it is. However, according to Midori, the amount of blood at the scene wasn't that little. It was said to be similar to the amount of blood Itou lost in 'Hell's Gate'."

McArthur seemed to have anticipated the detective's question and immediately answered, "As I said earlier, having a threatening letter would make it easier for people to understand why he went to the Inari house. Mukai-san probably thought that if he acted just because of an appointment letter without any content, it would seem suspicious."
Well, that makes sense logically, but it feels like he's being evasive.
"In any case, what he showed you wasn't a deduction. It was just a description of his own crime plan. Cutting off the foot, putting on the armor boots, chopping off the head, and placing it on the hat rack, all of it is the same as what I explained earlier, to create a space where Mukai-san's existence has no mystery. This way, he could maintain control over the entire case."
McCarto goes on and on.
"Now, let's take a look at the locked room. It's actually as simple as it gets. Because it's too simple, no one realized it, I suppose. No, I'm sure they must have thought of it. However, Woodside-san always said, 'This killer is clever and uses extraordinary methods,' so you all went off track, thinking that the locked room couldn't be that simple and the killer must have used more intelligence."
"But, just like a math problem, the answer is simple. The killer – Woodside-san's accomplice – locked the door from the outside of 'Hell's Gate' with Ito's key. Then, when the body was discovered, Woodside-san quickly placed the key in the hand of Mr. Yamane. Detective, who was the first to find the room key?"
"… Woodside-san."
I remember the scene.
Indeed, it was Kumotaka who first touched the corpse of Hama in the "Gate of Hell," and then found the key in his left hand while everyone was focused on Ito's head.

"I turned to the page that was open, which talked about various ways of killing, such as making a wax effigy to represent the victim and then slowly melting it with heat - or using a needle to pierce the wax effigy's heart, which would cause the person to die. Later, I heard from Mrs. Redfern that Linda Marshall bought candles early in the morning on the day of the murder, and she seemed embarrassed when it was discovered what she had bought. I can clearly imagine the scene that followed. Linda made a wax effigy - perhaps adding a small bundle of Eleanor's red hair to strengthen the magic - and then pierced the heart with a needle, put it in the fireplace, placed some paper scraps and cardboard underneath, lit a fire, and melted the wax effigy.
"This behavior was childish and superstitious, but it showed one thing: the desire to kill. What if this desire was not just in her mind? Could Linda Marshall have really killed her stepmother? At first, it seemed like she had a perfect alibi - but in fact, as I pointed out earlier, the time evidence was provided by Linda herself, and she may have exaggerated the time by fifteen minutes.
"It is very likely that once Mrs. Redfern left the beach, Linda followed her and went up the mountain, crossed the narrow ridge, ran down the ladder, found her stepmother on the beach, strangled her, and climbed back up the ladder before Miss Bustle and Patrick Redfern's boat arrived. She could have gone back to the gull bay, swam, and then returned to the hotel when she felt it was appropriate."

"However, as I have said before, I soon encountered an insurmountable obstacle. Patrick Redfern could not have killed her because he was with us on the beach first, and then with Miss Bustle on the ship before the body was discovered. So I had to take a different approach to thinking. There are several other possibilities, such as her husband - with the help of Miss Darnley - because they were both lying about something suspicious. She could have been silenced because she accidentally stumbled upon a smuggler. It could also have been done by a religious fanatic. Alternatively, it could have been her stepdaughter. This last point once led me to believe it was the truth. Linda's attitude during her first police interrogation was suspicious. Later, when I spoke to her again, it further convinced me that Linda thought she was guilty."
"Are you saying that she believed herself to have actually killed Elena just because she imagined it?" asked Rosamond in a tone of disbelief.

"I've been looking forward to meeting Miss Dunn. I buy a lot of things at Rossmond's, and I'm sure she's the owner, isn't she? I think she's a charming woman, how well she dresses, how well she puts together an outfit that makes her look so good. The outfit I wore last night was bought from her store. I think, from any angle, she's a lovely woman."
Colonel Barron, sitting next to Miss Bustard, had been shamelessly staring at the swimsuit models, and he muttered, "She seems like a refined woman."
Mrs. Gardner continued to knit her needles, "Honestly, Mr. Poirot, seeing you here has given me an idea - not that I'm not excited to see you, because I am, and Mr. Gardner knows it - but I can't help but wonder, you know, that you might be here for professional reasons. You understand what I mean, don't you? Oh, I'm just too sensitive, Mr. Gardner will tell you how sensitive I am, and if I get involved in any crime, I can't stand it. You know -"
"You know, Mr. Poirot, Mrs. Gardner is very sensitive."
Hercule Poirot waved his hand in the air. "Then rest assured, madam, my purpose here is the same as yours - to relax and enjoy a holiday. I haven't thought about solving any cases."
"There are no bodies on Pirate Island," said Miss Bustle stiffly.
"Ah, that may not be the case," said Hercule Poirot, pointing to the beach below. "Look at them, lying there in rows. What do they look like? Men and women? They look like nothing but - bodies[2]!"
"They look pretty good, some of them are quite attractive, though some are a bit thin," said Major Barry appreciatively.

"I agree, it has a romantic atmosphere," said Hercule Poirot. "It's peaceful, sunny, and the water is blue. But you forgot, Miss Bustle, that evil exists even under the sun."
The clergyman shifted in his seat and leaned forward, his blue eyes sparkling with interest. Miss Bustle shrugged. "Oh! I understand that, but…"
"But regardless, you still think this place isn't where a crime would happen, Miss Bustle. You forgot one thing."
"You mean human nature, I suppose?"
"There is a human element, of course, but that's not what I'm talking about. What I'm pointing out is that everyone who comes here comes for a vacation."
Emily Buston stared at him in surprise. "I don't understand."
Hercule Poirot smiled kindly at her and made a gesture with his hand. "Let's say you have an enemy. If you go to his house, his office, or find him on the street—you need a reason, you need to explain what you're doing. But at the seaside, you don't need to do that. You come to Ledcot Bay because it's August—everyone comes to the seaside in August, it's a tradition. So, it's natural that you're here, Mr. Lenn, that the Major is here, that Mrs. Redding and her husband are here. It's all very natural because British people come to the seaside in August."
"Well," Miss Buston admitted, "that's a good point. But what about the Gardners? They're Americans."
Poirot smiled slightly. "Even Mrs. Gardner, as she told us, needed a place to relax. And since she's in Britain, she had to spend a night or two at the seaside – even if she had no other intention, just to show that she's a very sophisticated tourist. She loves to observe others."
Mrs. Redfern whispered, "I suppose you like to observe others too."
"Madame, I must confess that I do. I have observed many things."
She said thoughtfully, "You have seen – many things."

These words came out of nowhere and sounded almost comical, but Linda's face was stern and her expression was filled with anxiety, without any hint of joking. Christine Redfern was initially puzzled and looked at her curiously, realizing she was serious and there was nothing funny about it...
She took a breath and said, "Yes, I've had - I've had - exactly that feeling..."
Mr. Bratte said, "So, you're the famous detective, huh?"
They sat in the bar, which was Mr. Bratte's favorite place.
Hercule Poirot nodded, not at all modest. Mr. Bret continued, "So, why are you here – to investigate a case?"
"No, no, I'm here to relax, I'm on vacation."
Mr. Bret raised an eyebrow. "Is that all you can say?"
Poirot replied, "That's not necessarily the case."
Horace Bret said, "Well, come on, be honest with me, you don't have to worry about me. I'm a man of discretion, I won't say anything I hear, and I always have been. I wouldn't get involved unless I knew what was going on. But you know most people – they can't keep their mouths shut about rumors and gossip, and that's no good for someone in your line of work! So you must say you're here for a vacation and not for anything else."
Poirot asked, "Why don't you believe me?"
Mr. Bret closed one eye and said, "I've seen all kinds of people, and I know their ways. You should be in France, in Deauville, Le Touquet, or Royan, that's where you belong - your... what's the word? - your spiritual home."
Poirot sighed. He looked out the window, where rain was falling and mist was rolling in over the island. "Perhaps you're right! At least, those places have plenty of entertainment even when it's raining."

Hercule Poirot sat atop a small hill on the island, to the left of the sheer cliff that led down to Elphiston Bay. At the top of the ladder, there were several large rocks, and he noticed that if someone wanted to descend the ladder to the beach, they could first hide behind the pile of rocks. The cliff's overhang made it difficult to see the beach from above.
Poirot nodded thoughtfully, the pieces of the puzzle falling into place in his mind as he reviewed all the information he had gathered: the morning of Eleanor Marshall's murder at the beach, the various conversations people had, bits and pieces that didn't seem to fit together.
The night of the card game, he, Patrick Redfern, and Rosamond Dane were at the table, with Christine Redfern as the dealer. They were interrupted by a conversation in the lounge. Who else was in the lounge at the time? Who was absent?
The conversation he had with Christine on the cliff the night before the murder, and the scene he witnessed on his way back to the hotel.
Chanel No. 5 perfume.
A pair of nail clippers.
A fragment of a pipe.
A bottle thrown out the window.
A green calendar.
A pack of candles.
A mirror and a typewriter.
A bundle of yarn.
A girl's watch.
Drainage water from a bathtub.
These unrelated facts must be put in their proper places, arranged neatly, and seamlessly connected. Then, when each fact is in its rightful position, it's time to move on! Confirm the existence of evil on the island...
Evil...
He looks down at a sheet of paper typed out on a typewriter in his hand.
Nellie Parsons – found strangled in a thicket near Chobham, with no leads yet to any suspects.
Nellie Parsons?
Alice Corigan.
He carefully studies the details of Alice Corigan's case.

He admired her exceptional beauty, her graceful posture, and her confident demeanor. He liked her smooth, jet-black hair and her carefree smile. Of course, she cannot escape responsibility, and she is certainly related to her - but it is completely another matter. I believe that from the beginning to the end, she was and was destined to be a sacrifice. Because she is beautiful, because she is charming, because men's eyes follow her, people judge her to be the kind of woman who would disrupt life and corrupt souls. Emily saw Patrick Redford's face turn pale. He jumped out of the boat, and she followed suit. After pulling the boat ashore, they walked towards the stiff and silent white body below the cliff, with Patrick Redford leading the way and Emily Bruce following closely behind.
She saw bronze limbs, a white backless swimsuit, and red ringlets peeking out from under the green hat - except for two arms spread out to the sides, which looked very odd. Indeed, they all relied on Gordon Claude. This did not mean that any family member was a parasite or idle. Jeremy Claude was a senior partner in a law firm, and Lionel Claude was a practicing physician.
However, behind the routine work and ordinary days, there was a solid financial cushion that made people feel comfortable. There was never a need for thrift or saving. The future was secure. Gordon Claude, a widower without children, would take care of everything. He had told everyone, and not just once, that it was a done deal.
His widowed sister, Adela Marchmont, might have moved into a smaller, more manageable house, but she stayed in the White House. Lin En attended elite schools. She had the opportunity to accept any expensive training she desired, thanks to the regular checks from her Gordon uncle.
Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."
Yes, Lynn thought, there were already enough relatives. Perhaps sometimes it would feel a little too much?
"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. In fact, he even sent me a most beautiful Venetian lace tablecloth from Italy."
"It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

Although she had enjoyed her time abroad, it was nice to leave the Women's Royal Naval Service and become a free woman again. The job had been interesting, with various social events and amusing, yet there were also tedious routines and the feeling of being confined with her comrades, which sometimes made her want to escape.
It was during that time that she longed for Wormsley Valley and this shabby yet cool and comfortable house, and her dear mother.
Lyn had a love-hate relationship with her mother. When she was far away from home, she loved her more, and the annoying things were put aside, and even if she remembered them, they only made her more homesick. Dear mother, she could drive you crazy! If only she didn't have to listen to her mother's voice, so sweet and melodious, but full of complaints, pronouncing the same old clichés over and over again.
She was here now, having completed her service, free, and back in White House. She had been home for three days, and an inexplicable dissatisfaction and restlessness were creeping up on her. Everything was the same - almost unchanged - the house, her mother, Rolly, the farm, and the family. The only thing that was different and shouldn't be was herself...
"Darling..." Mrs. Marchmont's delicate call came from downstairs. "Would you like me to bring a tray of breakfast to your room?"
Lynn called out loudly:
"No, thank you. I'll come down."
"Why," she thought, "mom insists on saying 'my daughter.' That's too silly!"

"Well, you see, André had some quite peculiar ideas. Maybe it was a kind of chivalry—or maybe for some other reason—but let's just assume that at some point in the past, making everyone think André was dead would have been beneficial. He was very good at manipulating the local natives—always has been. He could make up a convincing story, complete with detailed explanations, and let it spread. "That seems like too far-fetched an assumption to me," David said.
"Really? Is it?" Judd smiled. He leaned forward, gently patting David's knee, "What if all of that were true, Hunter? What if it were all true?"
"I would require concrete evidence."
"Would you? Well, of course, there wouldn't be a foolproof piece of evidence. André himself might appear here—in the Wormsley Valley. What do you think of that as evidence?"
"That would be undeniable," David said coldly.
"Oh, yes, undeniable—just a little awkward—I mean for Mrs. Gordon-Claude. Of course, because then she couldn't be Mrs. Gordon-Claude anymore. A bit awkward, wouldn't you say?"
"My sister," David said, "she was genuinely remarried."

"You don't agree?" Poirot asked. "Oh, well, perhaps I'm being too imaginative. Let's look at it this way. André arrived at Stagg. He wrote a letter to David Hunter. Hunter received the letter the next morning – at breakfast time, wasn't it?"
"Yes, that's right. He admitted to receiving a letter from Yatton."
"That's the first hint, isn't it? The hint that André Dahl had already arrived in the Vale of Worms? What was the first thing he did—he rushed his sister off to London!"
"That's quite understandable," Spence said. "He wanted to be free to handle things his way. He may have been worried that a woman would be too indecisive. Remember, he was always the dominant one. Mrs. Claud was completely under his control."

"But that's not surprising at all, Mr. Poirot. Rosalind Hunter married André in Cape Town and went straight to Nigeria with him. Hunter and André had never met. So, as you said, although Hunter suspected Yatton was André, he couldn't be sure—because he had never seen the man."

Michael O'Keefe, the farmer, arrived at the crime scene about an hour later. Van, or Old Pete, cleverly pretended to slowly walk along the road towards the intersection. He greeted O'Keefe, who invited him to get in the car, and then they discovered the corpse... As for the rest, Van calmly said, "Mr. Quin attended the interrogation, and you all know about it."
"Did you notify your brothers?"
"Yes. After finding Clinton's body at the crossroads, I hastily wrote a brief letter to Thomas—the one you call Thomas Brad—at my home. When we excitedly arrived in town, I managed to slip the letter through the mail slot—the post office was still closed. In the letter, I simply told Tom what happened and warned him that Crowsley was probably bent on revenge. I wrote that from then on, I would be Old Pitt, and neither he nor Stephen should mention it. I, at least, wanted to protect myself from Crowsley's wrath—because I am dead."
"You're lucky," Megala says bitterly, "When Tom received your letter, because he couldn't reach me, he must have written that note to the police—as a final warning to me before anything happened to me before I got back to Bradwood."
The two brothers look pale and tense; they are under immense pressure, both physically and mentally. Megala even becomes disoriented. They are startled when a hoarse laugh comes from outside the deck, only to realize that it is one of the crew members of the Helen mocking a policeman.
"Well," Esam finally says hopelessly, "Knowing the truth is good, but what good does it do us? It's still impossible to catch Crowsley."
"This is too pessimistic," Ellery said. "This is an excuse for one's own incompetence. Gentlemen, does anyone now or in the past know about the feud between the Tewell and Crosby families? A little investigation along that line may help us narrow down the suspects."

"I considered the possibility of Brad, but discarded it immediately: Brad's body had been confirmed by his widow, and there was a berry-shaped mole on the dead man's thigh. And for the same logical reasons, I also considered whether it could have been Meagal: no, it was impossible, as Temple had diagnosed Meagal's illness as a particular hernia, and Rumson had found the same type of hernia on the corpse hanging from the mast of the Helen. So, Brad and Meagal's bodies were indeed themselves. After excluding the extremely small possibility of a completely unknown person being involved, there were only two left – Wilga Crocass and Van's servant,
Ellery stopped to take a breath and continued, "Could the corpse be Croscot? Impossible. If it was Croscot, Van would not have gone to such great lengths to set up a deception; he could simply claim self-defense! He could have called the police, pointed out the corpse, and that would have been it. Given the background of the case, he would undoubtedly have been released. From Van's perspective, if he was innocent, that procedure was inevitable. And the fact that he did not do so proves that he could not do so. Why? Because the corpse was not Croscot's!
"If the corpse was not Croscot, it must be Clinton, the only remaining possibility. But Clinton was believed to have been killed in the murder case at the Arojo intersection seven months ago! Oh, but how did we know that the first corpse was Clinton? It was Van himself who said so, and he has now been proven to be the killer and a liar. We have every reason to believe that any statement Van makes that has not been verified is worth doubting. In this case, the facts point to the only possibility: the last corpse must have been Clinton's."

"Did you notify your brothers?"
"Yes. After finding Clinton's body at the crossroads, I hastily wrote a brief letter to Thomas—the one you call Thomas Brad—at my home. When we excitedly arrived in town, I managed to slip the letter through the mail slot—the post office was still closed. In the letter, I simply told Tom what happened and warned him that Crowsley was probably bent on revenge. I wrote that from then on, I would be Old Pitt, and neither he nor Stephen should mention it. I, at least, wanted to protect myself from Crowsley's wrath—because I am dead."
"You're lucky," Megala says bitterly, "When Tom received your letter, because he couldn't reach me, he must have written that note to the police—as a final warning to me before anything happened to me before I got back to Bradwood."
The two brothers look pale and tense; they are under immense pressure, both physically and mentally. Megala even becomes disoriented. They are startled when a hoarse laugh comes from outside the deck, only to realize that it is one of the crew members of the Helen mocking a policeman.
"Well," Esam finally says hopelessly, "Knowing the truth is good, but what good does it do us? It's still impossible to catch Crowsley."
"This is too pessimistic," Ellery said. "This is an excuse for one's own incompetence. Gentlemen, does anyone now or in the past know about the feud between the Tewell and Crosby families? A little investigation along that line may help us narrow down the suspects."

"I considered the possibility of Brad, but discarded it immediately: Brad's body had been confirmed by his widow, and there was a berry-shaped mole on the dead man's thigh. And for the same logical reasons, I also considered whether it could have been Meagal: no, it was impossible, as Temple had diagnosed Meagal's illness as a particular hernia, and Rumson had found the same type of hernia on the corpse hanging from the mast of the Helen. So, Brad and Meagal's bodies were indeed themselves. After excluding the extremely small possibility of a completely unknown person being involved, there were only two left – Wilga Crocass and Van's servant,
Ellery stopped to take a breath and continued, "Could the corpse be Croscot? Impossible. If it was Croscot, Van would not have gone to such great lengths to set up a deception; he could simply claim self-defense! He could have called the police, pointed out the corpse, and that would have been it. Given the background of the case, he would undoubtedly have been released. From Van's perspective, if he was innocent, that procedure was inevitable. And the fact that he did not do so proves that he could not do so. Why? Because the corpse was not Croscot's!
"If the corpse was not Croscot, it must be Clinton, the only remaining possibility. But Clinton was believed to have been killed in the murder case at the Arojo intersection seven months ago! Oh, but how did we know that the first corpse was Clinton? It was Van himself who said so, and he has now been proven to be the killer and a liar. We have every reason to believe that any statement Van makes that has not been verified is worth doubting. In this case, the facts point to the only possibility: the last corpse must have been Clinton's."

Chapter 1: Aroo's Christmas
The story begins at a crossroads, half a mile outside the small West Virginia village of Aroo, where one road leads from New Kensington to Pietown [1], and another leads to Aroo.
Ellery Queen immediately realized that the terrain was important. His first glance revealed many other things, but only found evidence conflicting and confusing. Everything seemed out of place, and it seemed necessary to leave the crossroads and think things over more carefully.
Ellery Queen, the erudite and cosmopolitan man, found himself standing in the cold and gloomy weather of the West Virginia handle region [2] at two o'clock in the afternoon on December 26th, next to an old Duesenberg [3] race car. This unusual phenomenon was caused by a combination of factors, with the most important being his father, Inspector Quin, who advocated working on holidays. The elderly man was deeply engrossed in his daily work, the so-called "police customs," and worked tirelessly. The crime situation in Chicago was always dire, and the police commissioner invited the top police officers from major cities to his jurisdiction to commiserate over the terrible state of affairs.
It was during the trip with his father, the Inspector, from the hotel to the Chicago Police Headquarters that Ellery learned about the perplexing case in Aroo, which was dubbed the "T-shaped murder" by the United Press. There were many elements in the report that piqued Ellery's interest - such as the fact that Andrew Van was decapitated and nailed to a cross on Christmas morning - that prompted him to pull his father out of the smoky Chicago meeting and drive off in a secondhand, fast Duesenberg towards the east.

"I thought you weren't interested," Ellery said, jumping off the sidewalk. "Hey, come here!" he called to a country bumpkin wrapped in a blue work suit, sweeping the sidewalk with a worn-out broom. "Is the sheriff of Arroyo here?" The man stared at him in disbelief. "Of course, it's written on the sign… come on, you crook."
It was a dreary residential area with few buildings. The Duesenberg stopped in front of a building whose skeletal structure was made of shoddy wood, like a box for growing mushrooms in the past. Next to it was a general store with an old gas pump in front, and then a car repair shop. A handwritten sign hung proudly in front of the mushroom box-shaped building: Arroyo Village Hall. They found the gentleman they were looking for sitting at a desk at the back of the building, asleep. The sign on the door read "Town Marshal."
Quinlan snorted, and the town marshal lifted his heavy eyelids, scratched his head, and said in a hoarse whisper, "If you're looking for Matt Hollis, he's out."
Ellery smiled. "We're looking for Arroyo's Sheriff Redden."
"Oh, I am," he said. "What do you want?"
"Sheriff," Ellery said menacingly, "allow me to introduce Richard Quin, the head of the New York Police Department's Homicide Division—he's here in person."
"Who?" The sheriff stared blankly, "New York?"
"Absolutely," Ellery said, stepping on his father's toes, "Now, Sheriff, we want—"
"Sit," said Sheriff Luddon, kicking a chair over to Quin. Quin grunted and sat down elegantly. "This Mr. Van's business, huh? I don't see how the New Yorkers would be interested. What's going on?"
Ellery took out a cigarette case and offered it to the sheriff, who grumbled and stuffed a large wad of chewing tobacco into his mouth.
"Tell me everything, Sheriff."

Quin: Don't waste time asking the hotel staff. There's all the necessary information here. A man resembling the description in the dossier arrived at the hotel around midnight yesterday and checked in. He left at 7:30 a.m. this morning by taxi. He gave up his limp, but the bandage on his wrist is a mystery. His clear trail indicates he's not afraid of being pursued; the driver told me he was going to Chinsville. I'm taking the train to Chinsville to catch up with him, and I'll leave further clues with the staff at the Clayton Hotel.
Yardeley
Ellery's eyes lit up, and he stuffed the note into his pocket. "When did Yardeley leave Stapletonville?"
"Around noon, sir, by taxi."
"Cheswick, is it?" Ellery pondered for a moment, then picked up the phone and said, "Connect me to the Chief of Police in Cheswick... Hello, police station? Let me speak to the chief... Hurry! Don't ask who I am... Hello! I'm Ellery Quincannon. The son of Detective Richard Quincannon of the New York Homicide Squad... Yes! I'm in Stapletonville, Chief, and I'm trailing a tall, dark-skinned man with a bandage on his wrist who took a taxi. The pursuer is a bearded tall man in another taxi... The first man is the killer... Yes! He left Stapletonville at 7:30 this morning... Well. I suppose you're right; he must have passed through there already. Please gather as much evidence as you can. The second man is unlikely to have reached Cheswick yet... Keep in touch with the Clayton Inn waiter. I'll be there as soon as I can."
He hung up the phone and rushed out of the Ford Stapletonville Hotel. The Duesenberg, like a Pony Express rider, galloped westward.
In Cheswick, Ellery quickly found the Clayton Inn, the inn's waiter, and a short, plump man in uniform who greeted him with a Rotary Club smile.
"How's it going?" Ellery asked.

A panoramic vision unfolded before Ellery's eyes. Due to a terrible oversight, the wheel of fate had turned, and his telegram to Redden was as good as unsent. The man in the checkered shirt patiently explained that the sheriff and the town's mayor, Matt Hollis, had left two days ago for their annual fishing trip; they would be gone for a week, camping out in the wilderness, fishing in the Ohio River and its tributaries. They wouldn't be back until Sunday. The telegram had arrived the day before, a few minutes past three; the man in the checkered shirt—who claimed to be the caretaker, housekeeper, and handyman—had received the telegram, signed it, and placed it on the sheriff's desk, where it might have sat for a week had Ellery not arrived. The caretaker seemed to have something on his mind, launching into a rambling discourse, but Ellery pushed him aside, his eyes filled with a vague fear, and returned to Aroon Street, jumping into his Duesenberg car.
He revved the engine, turned the corner, and drove along the route he remembered from his previous adventure with Esam and Sheriff Redden. There was no time to contact the county prosecutor, Krutem, or the state police's Captain Pike. If the thing he feared hadn't happened yet, he was sure he could handle any situation that might arise; he had a loaded semi-automatic pistol in the pocket of his Duesenberg. If it had already happened…
